'''Dorothy Jean Johnson Vaughan''' (September 20, 1910 – November 10, 2008) was an American [[mathematician]], [[human computer]], [[Programmer|computer programmer]] and [[Teacher|schoolteacher]] who worked for the [[National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics]] (NACA), and [[NASA]], at [[Langley Research Center]] in [[Hampton, Virginia]]. In 1949, she became acting supervisor of the [[West Area Computers]], the first African-American<!--"African American" should be in the lead, per Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Biographies#Context; it is a part of her WP:Notability.--> woman to receive a promotion and supervise a group of staff at the center.

She later was promoted officially to the position of supervisor. During her 28-year career, Vaughan prepared for the introduction of computers in the early 1960s by teaching herself and her staff the [[Fortran|Fortran programming language]]. She later headed the programming section of the Analysis and Computation Division (ACD) at Langley.

Vaughan is one of the women featured in [[Margot Lee Shetterly]]'s history ''[[Hidden Figures (book)|Hidden Figures: The Story of the African-American Women Who Helped Win the Space Race]]'' (2016). It was adapted as a [[Hidden Figures|biographical film]] of the same name, also released in 2016.

In 2019, Vaughan was honored with the [[Congressional Gold Medal]] posthumously.<ref name="congress">{{cite web |title=H.R.1396 - Hidden Figures Congressional Gold Medal Act |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/1396?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22hr1396%22%5D%7D&r=1&s=1 |website=Congress.gov |date = 8 November 2019|access-date=9 November 2019}}</ref>

==Career==
Vaughan graduated from Wilberforce University in 1929. Although encouraged by professors to do graduate study at [[Howard University]],<ref name="nymag"/> Vaughan worked as a mathematics teacher at [[R.R. Moton High School|Robert Russa Moton High School]] in [[Farmville, Virginia]], in order to assist her family during the [[Great Depression in the United States|Great Depression]].{{sfn|Shetterly|2016b|pp=21–22, 91–92}} During the 14 years of her teaching career, Virginia's public schools and other facilities were still racially segregated under [[Jim Crow laws]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |url=https://interestingengineering.com/dorothy-vaughan-nasas-human-computer-and-american-hero |title=Dorothy Vaughan: NASA's 'Human Computer' and American Hero |date=2018-03-11 |website=interestingengineering.com |access-date=2018-12-11}}</ref>

In 1935, [[Langley Research Center]] in [[Hampton, Virginia]], established its first female [[Computer (occupation)|computing]] pool.<ref name="nymag" /> In 1941, President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] issued [[Executive Order 8802]], to desegregate the defense industry, and [[Fair Employment Practice Committee|Executive Order 9346]] to end racial segregation and discrimination in hiring and promotion among federal agencies and defense contractors.<ref name=":2" /> These helped ensure the war effort drew from all of American society after the United States entered [[World War II]] in 1941. With the enactment of the two Executive Orders, and with many men being swept into service, federal agencies such as the [[National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics]] (NACA) also expanded their hiring and increased recruiting of women, including women of color, to support the war production of airplanes.<ref name="nymag">{{Cite web |url=http://nymag.com/thecut/2016/08/dorothy-vaughan-space-race-c-v-r.html
 |title=The Hidden Black Women Who Helped Win the Space Race |last=Shetterly |first=Margot Lee |year=2016a |work=[[New York (magazine)|New York]]}}</ref> Two years following the issuance of Executive Orders 8802 and 9346, the Langley Memorial Aeronautical Laboratory (Langley Research Center), a facility of the NACA, began hiring more Black women to meet the drastic increase in demand for processing aeronautical research data.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/content/dorothy-vaughan-biography |title=Dorothy Vaughan Biography |last1=Shetterly |first1=Margot Lee |last2=Loff |first2=Sarah |date=2016-11-22 |website=NASA |access-date=2018-12-11 |archive-date=2020-06-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200625171042/https://www.nasa.gov/content/dorothy-vaughan-biography/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> The US believed that the war was going to be won in the air. It had already ramped up airplane production, creating a great demand for engineers, mathematicians, craftsmen and skilled tradesmen.

In 1943, Vaughan began a 28-year-career as a [[Computer (occupation)|human computer]] and computer programmer at [[Langley Research Center]] where she came to perform calculations for [[flight path]]s, the [[Scout (rocket family)|Scout Project]], and [[computer programming]]. Her career in this field kicked off during the height of World War II. She came to the Langley Memorial Aeronautical Laboratory thinking that it would be a temporary war job. One of her children later worked at NACA.<ref name=Spelman>{{cite web |title= Hidden Figure: Dorothy Vaughan |url=http://www.spelman.edu/about-us/news-and-events/our-stories/hidden-figures/2016/11/22/hidden-figure-nasa-dorothy-vaughan |website=Spelman College |access-date=January 3, 2017}}</ref> Vaughan was assigned to the [[West Area Computers|West Area Computing]], a segregated unit, which consisted of only African Americans. This was due to prevailing [[Jim Crow laws]] that required newly hired African American women to work separately from their white women counterparts.<ref name=":3" /> They were also required to use separate dining and bathroom facilities.<ref name=":3" /> This segregated group consisted of African-American women who made complex mathematical calculations by hand, using tools of the time.<ref name="nymag" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |url=http://thehumancomputerproject.com/women/dorothy-vaughan |title=Dorothy Vaughan |website=The Human Computer Project |last=Shetterly |first=Margot Lee  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220704032654/http://thehumancomputerproject.com/women/dorothy-vaughan | archive-date=2022-07-04}}</ref>

Their work expanded in the postwar years to support research and design for the United States' space program, which was emphasized under President [[John F. Kennedy]]. In 1949, Vaughan was assigned as the acting head of the [[West Area Computers]], taking over from a woman who had died. She was the first Black supervisor at NACA and one of few female supervisors, leading a group composed entirely of African-American women.<ref name="NASA">{{cite web|url=http://crgis.ndc.nasa.gov/crgis/images/2/29/VaughanBio.pdf |title=Dorothy Vaughan (nee Johnson)|newspaper=NASA |date=3 February 2016|last1=Allen|first1=Bob}}</ref> She served for years in an acting role before being promoted officially to the position as supervisor.{{sfn|Shetterly|2016b|pp=21–22, 91–92}}

Vaughan moved into the area of electronic computing in 1961, after NACA introduced the first [[Digital computer|digital computers]] to the center. Vaughan became proficient in computer programming, teaching herself [[Fortran|FORTRAN]] and teaching it to her coworkers to prepare them for the transition. She contributed to the space program through her work on the [[Scout (rocket family)|Scout Launch Vehicle Program]].<ref name=":1"/>

Vaughan continued after [[NASA]], the successor agency, was established in 1958. When NACA became NASA, segregated facilities, including the West Computing office, were abolished. In a 1994 interview, Vaughan recalled that working at Langley during the [[Space Race]] felt like being on "the cutting edge of something very exciting".{{sfn|Golemba|1994|p=121}}  Regarding being an African American woman during that time in Langley, she remarked, "I changed what I could, and what I couldn't, I endured." Vaughan worked in the Numerical Techniques division through the 1960s. Dorothy Vaughan and many of the former West Computers joined the new Analysis and Computation Division (ACD), a racially and gender-integrated group on the frontier of electronic computing. She worked at NASA-Langley for 28 years.<ref name="NASA" />

During her career at Langley, Vaughan was also raising her six children, one of whom later also worked at NASA-Langley. Vaughan lived in [[Newport News, Virginia]], and commuted to work at Hampton via public transportation.

==Later years ==
[[File:L Dorothy Vaughan M Lessie Hunter R Vivian Adair.jpg|thumb|Vaughan with her [[human computer]] colleagues [[Lessie Hunter]], and [[Vivian Adair]]. [[Margaret Ridenhour]] and [[Charlotte Craidon]] are standing in the back.]]
Vaughan wanted to continue at another management position at NASA, but never received an offer.<ref name="Dorothy Johnson Vaughan">{{Cite web|title=Dorothy Johnson Vaughan|url=https://www.biography.com/scientist/dorothy-johnson-vaughan|access-date=2021-03-02|website=Biography|date=15 September 2020 |language=en-us}}</ref> She retired from NASA in 1971, at the age of 61. In her final decade of her career, she alongside [[Katherine Johnson|Katherine G. Johnson]] and [[Mary Jackson (engineer)|Mary Jackson]] helped calculate astronauts [[John Glenn]]'s launch into orbit,<ref name="Dorothy Johnson Vaughan"/> Neil Armstrong famous first step on the moon, and even the first American to be in space, Alan Shepard.<ref>{{Cite news|title=The Inspiring True Story of 'Hidden Figures': Meet the Real NASA Mathematicians Who Got Man on the Moon|url=https://people.com/inside-the-true-story-of-hidden-figures-8782551|work=People.com|access-date=2026-02-01}}</ref> She died on November 10, 2008, aged 98 and was buried at Hampton Memorial Gardens.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Webb |first=Jeffrey |date=2024-02-14 |title=Dorothy Vaughan |url=https://www.wvencyclopedia.org/entries/2429 |encyclopedia=e-WV: The West Virginia Encyclopedia Online |publisher=West Virginia Humanities Council |access-date=2025-03-31}}</ref> Vaughan was a member of [[Alpha Kappa Alpha]], an African-American sorority. She was also an active member of the [[African Methodist Episcopal Church]] where she participated in music and missionary activities.<ref>"Obituary: Dorothy Vaughan," ''Newport News,'' November 2008.</ref>

At the time of her death, she was survived by four of her six children, ten grandchildren and fourteen great-grandchildren.<ref name="blackpast.org">{{Cite web |url=http://www.blackpast.org/aah/vaughan-dorothy-johnson-1910-2008 |title=Vaughan, Dorothy Johnson (1910–2008) |website=The Black Past: Remembered and Reclaimed |access-date=2017-10-09|date=2017-01-07 }}</ref>

==Legacy==
Vaughan was the first Black female manager at [[NASA]]. As one of the first female [[Fortran|FORTRAN]] programmers, she instructed her peers and paved a way for female programmers at NASA.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Loff |first=Sarah |date=2016-11-22 |title=Dorothy Vaughan Biography |url=http://www.nasa.gov/content/dorothy-vaughan-biography |access-date=2023-04-01 |website=NASA |archive-date=2018-11-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181130144413/https://www.nasa.gov/content/dorothy-vaughan-biography/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2005, a scholarship fund with the Salem Community Foundation was created under Dorothy Vaughan’s name to further music training by the Salem Music Study Club.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Principal Funds |url=https://salemcommunityfoundation.org/index.php/principal-funds |access-date=2023-04-01 |website=salemcommunityfoundation.org}}</ref>

Vaughan is one of the women featured in [[Margot Lee Shetterly]]'s 2016 non-fiction book ''[[Hidden Figures (book)|Hidden Figures]]'', and the [[Hidden Figures|feature film of the same name]]. She was portrayed by the [[Academy Award]] winning actress [[Octavia Spencer]].

The Dorothy J. Vaughan Academy of Technology opened in [[Charlotte, North Carolina|Charlotte, NC]], in August 2017. This school is inspired by Vaughan’s “leadership, innovation, creativity, curiosity, and love of learning.” The school is a member of the Magnet Schools of America Association.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dorothy J. Vaughan Academy of Technology |url=https://www.cmsk12.org/domain/4896 |access-date=2023-04-01 |website=Charlotte–Mecklenburg Schools |language=en }}</ref>

In 2019, Vaughan was awarded the [[Congressional Gold Medal]].<ref name="congress"/>  Also in 2019, the [[Vaughan (crater)|Vaughan crater]] on the far side of the Moon was named in her honor.

On 6 November 2020, a satellite named after her (ÑuSat 12 or "Dorothy", COSPAR 2020-079D of the [[ÑuSat]] series) was launched into space.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2020-079A | title=NASA - NSSDCA - Spacecraft - Details }}</ref>

Vaughan’s personal Bible and NASA retirement identification card are displayed in the Museum of the Bible’s exhibition ''Scripture and Science: Our Universe, Ourselves, Our Place.'' <ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=No Longer Hidden: The Legacy of Dorothy Vaughan |url=https://www.museumofthebible.org/magazine/featured/no-longer-hidden-the-legacy-of-dorothy-vaughan |access-date=2023-04-01 |website=Museum of the Bible |language=en-US}}</ref> The [[African Methodist Episcopal Church]] also gave her a service award.<ref name=":0" /> 

[[North Central University]] has a scholarship in honor of Dorothy Vaughan for [[Person of color|BIPOC]] and/or female students.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dorothy Vaughan Scholarship |url=https://www.northcentral.edu/dorothy-vaughan-scholarship/ |access-date=2023-04-01 |website=North Central University |language=en}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* 1925: Beechurst High School – Class Valedictorian
* 1925: West Virginia Conference of the A.M.E. Sunday School Convention – Full Tuition Scholarship
* 1929: Wilberforce University – Mathematician Graduate Cum Laude
* 1949–1958: Head of National Advisory Committee of Aeronautics' Segregated West Computing Unit (NACA)
* October 16, 2019: [[Vaughan (crater)|a lunar crater]] is named after her.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/15862 |title=Vaughan |website=Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> This name was chosen by [[planetary scientist]] [[Ryan N. Watkins]] and her student, and submitted on what would have been Dorothy Vaughan's 109th birthday.<ref>Ryan Watkins, [https://twitter.com/Ryan_N_Watkins/status/1184557602447020034?s=19 "Thrilled to announce that this small (3 km) crater on the Moon now has a name - Vaughan! My student and I chose to name Vaughan crater after Dorothy Vaughan (you may remember her from @HiddenFigures, where she was portrayed by @octaviaspencer)."], ''Twitter'', 16 octobre 2019.</ref>
* November 8, 2019: [[Congressional Gold Medal]]<ref name="congress" /> which was accepted by family members at the 2024 ceremony<ref>{{cite web | title=NASA's Hidden Figures Honored with Congressional Gold Medals | website=NASA | date=September 19, 2024 | url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/langley/nasas-hidden-figures-honored-with-congressional-gold-medals | access-date=September 20, 2024}}</ref>
* On November 6, 2020, a satellite named after her was launched into space<ref>{{cite web | url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2020-079A | title=NASA - NSSDCA - Spacecraft - Details }}</ref>
* On July 19, 2024, NASA Johnson Space Center's central data office, known as Building 12, was renamed as the "Dorothy Vaughan Center in Honor of the Women of Apollo" as a "tribute to the people who made humanity's first steps on the Moon possible."<ref> "Cone, Allen, "NASA Johnson Space Center to dedicate building to Dorothy Vaughan, women of Apollo", UPI, July 15, 2024.</ref>§
